column4: The section quotes this soil comparison: good land brings forth its plants by its Lord’s permission, while corrupt land yields only sparingly; the ending addresses those who give thanks. It makes the barren kenūd soil an image of a response that withholds what care could produce.

The section’s root ث و ر glosses the wind’s action as raising clouds; this ayah says the winds stir up سحاب and the clouds bring rain. The verbal and weather scene shows the first link in the nurturing chain.

The section’s K-N-D dictionary gloss says the ingrate counts afflictions and forgets favors. Here God’s نعمة cannot be counted, yet the human is called unjust and ungrateful; the contrast corrects what a person chooses to count.

The section says a person cuts the return of gratitude to the giver. This ayah names the human as كفور after God rescues people from distress at sea and they turn away on reaching land, making the severed response concrete.

The section asks what it means to be ungrateful to one’s Rabb after receiving care and gifts. This direct address asks what deludes the human against the generous Lord, joining the same human, Rabb, and forgotten generosity.
The section sets the gift of care against kenūd ingratitude. This ayah says the way was shown, then names the two responses as شاكرا or كفورا; it makes the severed bond a chosen response.

The section allows 100:7’s witness to refer to the human or to the Rabb. Here God asks “ألست بربكم” and the people answer “شهدنا”; it supplies a remembered testimony to the Rabb as the relation later denied.
The section’s kenūd person fails to return thanks for nourishment. This town had أمن and رزق from every place, then met the consequence of kufr; the provision and failed response occupy one scene.
The section calls gratitude the return that is cut off. This ayah directly contrasts شكر with kufr and says thanks brings increase, giving the severed return a stated consequence.

The section’s Rab dictionary gloss describes the one who nurtures, while its field scene moves from rain to gardens. This ayah asks who sends water and grows gardens whose trees people cannot grow; it locates the harvest’s source beyond the farmer.

The section develops kenūd land as soil that produces nothing. This ayah points to dead earth revived and grain brought out for people to eat, making the contrast between withheld and yielded nourishment visible.

The section names the farmer in its root خ ب ر gloss and describes land worked for a crop. This ayah asks whether people have considered what they sow or plow (تحرثون), focusing attention on the human labor in that field.
The section’s farmer works soil that may still be kenūd. This ayah asks whether people make the crop grow or God does, distinguishing cultivation from the power that completes its yield.

The section places rainfall among the gifts that call for thanks. After asking about water from rain clouds in 56:68–69, this ayah says God could make it bitter and asks why they do not give thanks; it makes water’s dependence and the proper return explicit.

The section’s dictionary gloss for ن ق ع includes floodwater gathering, and its image asks what care yields. This ayah stages rain-fed valleys carrying foam that passes while what benefits people remains; it gives the collected-water image a distinction between transient and lasting yield.

The section’s field depends on a Rabb who raises life through stages. This ayah directs attention to God’s mercy in reviving earth after its death; the dead-to-living contrast shows what the nurturing relation can bring about.

The section links wind, cloud, rain, and a dead field. This ayah describes God sending winds that stir clouds and driving them to a dead land, then reviving the earth; it closely restages that sequence.

The section’s field scene begins with wind and rain as provision. This ayah names the winds as glad tidings before mercy and the water sent down from heaven, showing the gift arriving before the land’s yield.

The section says water and soil can nourish what becomes a crop. This ayah explains that the rain gives life to a dead land and provides drink for cattle and people; it extends the field’s yield to living recipients.

The section assembles wind, cloud, water, and earth into a chain of care. This ayah places the winds, clouds, rain, and revived earth together among God’s signs, with a concluding call to reason; it lets the reader see the whole field relation at once.

The section names grain in its ح ب ب dictionary entry and describes soil’s failure to produce. This ayah says God splits the grain and date-stone and brings the living from the dead, locating crop and renewed life in the same act.

The section’s wheat-and-barley grain gloss and rain-fed field are both present here: water descends, plants grow, and grain, dates, grapes, and olives appear. The abundance shows what the kenūd land refuses to yield.

The section’s cloud-and-field chain turns on rain reaching the earth. This ayah names water sent down from the sky as drink and as the means for pasture and trees to grow, showing how provision starts.

The section names the grain expected from cared-for soil. This ayah says rain produces crops, olives, palms, grapes, and other fruits; it supplies specific forms of the yield the barren land withholds.

The section’s dictionary glosses for ن ق ع and خ ب ر describe water gathered and retained in low earth. This ayah says water is sent down in measure and lodged in earth, while God can take it away; it sharpens both gathering and dependence.

The section describes a farmer and the grain promised by good soil. This ayah names gardens of date palms and grapes, abundant fruit, and food from them; it gives the cultivated yield a concrete form.

The section’s field depends on water that nurtures growth. This ayah calls the rain water blessed and says it grows gardens and grain to harvest; it makes the same provision-to-crop movement explicit.
The section specifically names the farmer’s yield and grain. This ayah continues the rain-grown scene with tall date palms bearing clustered fruit, giving a particular image of completed growth.

The section links a land’s yield to nourishment for living beings. This ayah calls the crops provision for servants and says rain revives dead land; the harvest becomes a gift received, not merely a field’s output.
The section describes a farmer working soil and awaiting its yield. This ayah says water is poured down abundantly before the earth is split, presenting the first physical steps toward the crop.
The section’s grain image is developed here: after water, the earth is split open. This ayah gives the ground’s opening as the immediate scene that makes growth possible.
The section explicitly names the grain حبة in wheat and barley. This ayah names grain among the foods brought out of the earth, joining the dictionary detail to a crop scene.
The section expects a fruitful field after rain. This ayah adds grapes and fodder to the earth’s yield, showing that the provision extends beyond grain.
The section names the farmer and the crop-bearing land. This ayah names olives and palms among the yield, making the cared-for field visible as a varied orchard.
The section’s image depends on ground that gives growth. This ayah adds enclosed gardens to the sequence of what the earth brings forth, extending the scene from staple crop to cultivated abundance.
The section asks what a field’s care can yield. This ayah names fruit and pasture, completing a list of nourishment provided for people and animals.
The section says land’s growth is a gift that can be received and forgotten. This ayah concludes that food and enjoyment are for people and their livestock, naming the recipients of the provision.
The section names clouds that nourish plants and rain that reaches the ground. This ayah describes abundant water poured from rain clouds, the direct source of the field’s growth.
The section names grain as the expected yield from cared-for soil. This ayah connects rain to the production of grain and plants, giving the scene’s hoped-for harvest.
The section’s farmer works for a yield from the land. This ayah adds thick gardens to the rain-fed scene, a visible instance of soil that does produce.

The section’s ر ب ب dictionary gloss defines nurturing as bringing something along state by state toward completion. This ayah begins the human’s created stages from an extract of clay, a bodily parallel to that gradual making.
The section describes nurturing as a process moving through successive states. This ayah places the human drop in a secure resting place, continuing the bodily sequence from the prior verse.

The section’s dictionary definition of التربية is creation state by state toward completion. This ayah names successive stages of human formation and their final creation; it makes that sense of nurture explicit.

The section connects a nurturing Lord with land revived after rain. This ayah joins human formation through stages to barren earth stirred by water and growing every kind; both images make gradual formation visible.
The section’s root ر ب ب gloss describes bringing something through successive states to completion. This ayah says God created people in stages (أطوارا), a concise parallel to that dictionary sense.
The section defines Rabb’s nurturing as creating successively and bringing toward completion. This ayah says God created and proportioned, naming formation as an ordered act of care.
The section describes nurturing as measured development toward an end. This ayah says God decreed and guided, adding direction to the process of formation.
The section’s Rab gloss includes the one who improves and nurtures. Moses identifies his Lord as the one who gave each thing its creation and then guided it, making care both fitting and directing.

The section’s ر ب ب dictionary gloss includes completing a given blessing. This ayah says God will complete His favor upon Joseph and the family of Jacob, naming the same movement from gift to completion.

The section says a blessing can be brought to completion through Rabb-like care. This ayah says God completed His favor and perfected the religion that day, giving completion of favor a direct Qur’anic formulation.
The section’s root gloss associates Rabb with completing a blessing. This ayah says God completes His favor upon people through shade, shelter, and protection, supplying concrete forms of care.

The section’s field image joins land, provision, and the human response of thanks. This ayah describes Sheba’s two gardens and tells them to eat their Lord’s provision and give thanks; it makes the reciprocity explicit.

The section describes water as a condition of fruitful land. This ayah says a flood was sent upon Sheba and their two gardens were replaced by bitter-fruited ones; water and land turn from provision to loss.

The section calls human ingratitude a failure to answer provision. This ayah identifies the people’s kufr as the reason for recompense after the garden account, making the field’s failure a moral boundary as well.
The section pictures rain completing the care of a field. This ayah promises abundant rain in response to seeking forgiveness, showing provision arriving from above.
The section connects divine care with fertile ground. This ayah continues the promise with wealth, children, gardens, and rivers, laying out a full scene of gifts that could be acknowledged.

The section names grain (حبة) and says a good yield is the expected return of care. This ayah compares a charitable gift to a seed grain producing seven ears, joining crop and generosity as multiplied return.
The section’s good-soil image is paired here with spending for God’s approval: a garden on a height receives rain and yields twice over. It shows a generous response taking root in receptive ground.

The section says a person loves خير, which its dictionary entry glosses as gift and generosity. This ayah says righteousness is not attained until one spends what one loves; it turns attachment to good into a response of giving.
The section describes harvested grain and care of the land. This ayah says to eat the crop when it bears fruit and give its due on harvest day, linking yield with a return to others.

The section describes gifts whose source the recipient forgets. Solomon identifies an extraordinary gift as a trial of whether he will be grateful or ungrateful, giving a clear model of recognizing the giver.

The section depicts ingratitude as failing to answer a gift. Luqman is given wisdom and told to give thanks; the ayah adds that gratitude benefits the grateful person, clarifying the relation’s consequence.

The section says gratitude is the response to provision but easily withheld. Solomon’s household is told to work in gratitude, and the verse says few servants are grateful; it makes gratitude a practical return for gifts.

The section says the receiver cuts the return of thanks to the giver. This ayah tells believers to eat the good provisions God gave them and be grateful to Him, directly naming the reciprocal response.

The section’s خير includes gifts and generosity, and its field scene yields food. This ayah tells people to eat God’s lawful, good provision and thank Him for His favor, joining nourishment to gratitude.

The section says a person can forget the Rabb behind a gift. This ayah states that every blessing people have is from God, then says they call upon Him in distress; it identifies the giver before the human response.
The section describes land sustaining a person while the person is kenūd to the Rabb. This ayah says God established people on earth and provided means of livelihood, then says few give thanks.
The section calls human beings ungrateful to their Rabb despite what they receive. This ayah names hearing, sight, and hearts given by God, followed by the observation that people give little thanks.

The section says the human forgets gifts while failing to thank their giver. This ayah names hearing, sight, and hearts given to people as they emerge from their mothers, with the purpose that they may be grateful.
The section sees ordinary care as a gift whose source is forgotten. This ayah names night for rest and day for sight, then says most people do not give thanks for God’s favor.
The section’s K-N-D gloss says the ingrate counts troubles and forgets gifts. This ayah says if people count God’s favors they cannot enumerate them, giving the opposite scale of what is forgotten.

The section describes a person measuring what he receives while forgetting the giver. This ayah says the person reads abundant provision as proof that his Lord honored him; it exposes one way gifts can be misread.

The section connects kenūd with counting hardship instead of remembering care. This ayah says a person reads restricted provision as proof that his Lord humiliated him, completing the mistaken measure begun in 89:15.

The section’s ingrate receives care but does not return it. This ayah rejects the claim that provision alone signals honor and names failure to honor the orphan, bringing the question of response into social action.
The section’s kenūd figure breaks reciprocity after receiving gifts. This ayah says people do not urge one another to feed the poor, naming a withheld form of generosity.

The section’s word حبّ is paired with خير and its dictionary gloss includes gift or wealth. This ayah says people love wealth intensely (حبّ المال), giving a concrete instance of attachment to material good.
The section says the kenūd person counts calamities. This ayah describes the human as distressed when touched by evil, one side of a response that measures what is lost.
The section says the kenūd person forgets blessings. This ayah says the human withholds when good touches him, showing how receiving a gift can end in non-return.

The section says the human clings intensely to خير and forgets the giver. This ayah depicts a person gathering wealth and counting it, a specific, though indirect, picture of attachment that measures possession rather than relationship.

The section’s Rab gloss includes sustaining and completing gifts. This ayah recalls that God found the Prophet in need and made him self-sufficient, a concrete instance of care provided rather than self-made.
The section asks what response a recipient owes the Rabb. This ayah commands the Prophet to speak of his Lord’s favor, a direct example of acknowledging the giver.

The section says a person forgets gifts and cuts the return of gratitude. This ayah says that after God removes distress and grants favor, the person forgets the plea and assigns partners; it states the severance plainly.

The section says the human loves what he receives but forgets its giver. This ayah says that after favor reaches him, he claims it came through his own knowledge, a specific way of obscuring the Rabb’s hand.

The section describes the human as ungrateful to the one who cares for him. This ayah says that when favor is bestowed he turns away, but when evil touches him he makes lengthy supplication, a reversal in his response to ease and distress.

The section links receiving mercy to a failure to answer the Rabb. This ayah says that when people taste mercy they rejoice, but when their own hands have sent ahead evil they become ungrateful; it shows the unstable response to provision.

The section describes the recipient who forgets the giver after receiving خير. This ayah says a person turns aside when favored but despairs when touched by evil, echoing the section’s contrast between gifts and counted afflictions.
The section says the human can count loss and forget earlier care. This ayah describes despair when mercy is withdrawn after the person has tasted it, a concrete reversal in how favor is remembered.

The section depicts ingratitude to the Rabb after gifts. This ayah describes boastful rejoicing after hardship is removed, showing a human response that treats restored ease as self-evident rather than as care.
The section asks why a person is kenūd to his Rabb despite ongoing nurture. This ayah says the human transgresses, naming the response that follows.
The section’s claim of ingratitude is explained here: the human transgresses when he sees himself as self-sufficient (استغنى). It names the illusion that cuts the felt relation to the Rabb.

The section treats favor as a sustained relation that can be answered or severed. This ayah says God does not change a favor bestowed on a people until they change what is within themselves, making the response part of the relation.

The section names the human’s ingratitude to the Rabb. This ayah says people call on God sincerely aboard a ship but associate others with Him once safely brought to land, matching the rescue-and-turning pattern.

The section turns on what the earth produces under care. This ayah itself asks the human to look at his food; 80:25 supplies the rain-and-soil sequence, so this row contributes the question that directs attention to the source of food.

The section’s خير dictionary gloss includes gift and wealth. This ayah calls wealth and children ornaments of worldly life but says enduring good deeds are better with the Lord, distinguishing a received good from what lasts.

The section’s K-N-D dictionary gloss includes refusing continued closeness. This ayah describes people who break God’s covenant and cut what He ordered to be joined, giving the severed bond a communal and moral form.

The section’s K-N-D gloss includes ingratitude to maintaining a bond. This ayah describes breaking covenant and cutting what God ordered joined; it makes the image of severed reciprocity a concrete breach.

The section’s dictionary sense of K-N-D includes refusing continuing closeness. This ayah asks whether people will turn away and cut their kinship ties, extending the image of broken connection to family relations.

The section names the human’s ingratitude after distress has passed. This ayah stages people calling to God in a storm at sea; 10:23 supplies the specific post-rescue transgression, while this row contributes the desperate plea.

The section says the person cuts gratitude after receiving care. This ayah says that once God saves people to land they transgress; 10:22 supplies their plea at sea, while this row gives the turning-away response.

The section’s image joins distress and remembered care. This ayah says people call on their Lord when harm touches them, even though the resulting response to mercy is described in 30:34; this row contributes the appeal.
The section says people fail to return thanks for gifts. This ayah says some associate partners after God lets them taste mercy; 30:33 supplies the distress-and-appeal preceding this row.

The section describes an ingrate who counts distress and forgets blessings. This ayah says a person calls upon God when harm touches him, then passes on as though he had never called once harm is removed, making forgetfulness explicit.

The section sets the human’s intense love of خير against his attention to calamity. This ayah says the person does not tire of asking for good but despairs when evil touches him, a direct imbalance in what is remembered.

The section says the human forgets the giver after receiving a gift. This ayah describes a person claiming favor as his own and doubting the Hour; the self-attribution makes ingratitude more than a missed thank-you.
The section says the Rabb remains fully informed of those who cut the bond. This ayah says the earth will report its news on that day, adding the ground itself as a witness in the reckoning.
The section moves from a human witness to the Rabb’s knowledge on the final day. This ayah says whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, making hidden conduct visible.
The section says the Rabb is fully informed of people on that day. This ayah says whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it, completing the exposure of what had seemed uncounted.
The section says the human may be the witness in 100:7. This ayah says a person is a witness against himself, directly supporting that reading of the pronoun.
The section frames witness as knowledge that cannot be cut away by denial. This ayah says a person’s excuses do not erase that self-witness, extending the accountability in 75:14.
The section allows the human to be witness to his own ingratitude. This ayah says people’s hearing, sight, and skins testify against them, supplying bodily witnesses to deeds.
The section connects testimony with known human conduct. This ayah says tongues, hands, and feet testify against people for what they used to do, making the witness physical and specific.
The section says the human’s testimony may be directed against himself. This ayah says hands speak and feet testify to what people earned, a bodily disclosure of the actions at issue.
The section brings what is inside the chest to account in 100:10. This ayah names the day when hidden things are tested and exposed, a direct parallel to disclosed inward contents.

The section says the Rabb knows those who cut the gratitude bond and the surah asks what is within graves and chests. This ayah lays out the record and says no small or great deed is left uncounted, making that knowledge exhaustive.
The section says the Rabb is fully informed of people’s deeds. This ayah says guardians are appointed over them, giving a concrete form to the witnessed record.
The section develops a witness grounded in knowledge. This ayah calls the recorders noble writers, identifying who preserves what is done.
The section says those who cut the bond remain within the Rabb’s knowledge. This ayah says the recorders know what people do, a specific witness to their conduct.

The section says the Rabb is fully informed of people on that day. This ayah says God knows what is in the heavens and earth and what people conceal or declare, connecting hidden contents with divine knowledge.
The section says the Rabb knows those who act as though their ingratitude can be hidden. This ayah says God knows what is concealed in breasts as well as what is declared, extending the image inward.
The section calls the Lord خبير, fully informed. This ayah asks whether the One who created would not know, and calls Him لطيف خبير; it links creating and knowing the inward person.

The section says the Rabb is fully informed of people and names the contents of the chest. This ayah says God knows the unseen of the heavens and earth and what breasts conceal, directly connecting hiddenness and knowledge.

The section says those who cut the bond do not leave their Lord’s knowledge. This ayah says no matter what people do, their Lord is witness over them and nothing is hidden from Him, making that claim concrete.

The section connects the Rabb’s knowledge to the field’s grain and leaves. This ayah says no leaf falls without God knowing it and mentions a grain in the darkness of earth; the same growth scene remains fully within divine knowledge.

The section’s dictionary senses include water gathered in low earth and a farmer working soil. This ayah describes rain entering springs, crops growing, then yellowing and becoming debris; it shows both nourishing growth and its passing.
The section describes a field whose soil may fail to yield. This ayah shows dry earth stirred by rain until it swells and produces, a vivid reversal from lifelessness to growth.
The section says rain completes care of the land. This ayah says God sends water in measure and revives a dead land with it, joining measured provision to renewed growth.
The section places winds and water in the chain of field care. This ayah names winds and rain that revives earth after its death among God’s signs, tying the scene to recognition of the giver.
The section’s cloud, rain, and plant scene is named across roots and prose. This ayah says winds are sent as fertilizing and water is sent down, a close parallel to weather sustaining growth.

The section’s field image makes a yield-bearing garden a sign of care and response. This ayah itself frames the owners’ garden as a test; 68:24 later supplies their decision to bar the poor, so this row contributes the garden-as-test setting.

The section’s K-N-D gloss includes cutting a continuing relation. In this garden parable, the owners whisper that no poor person should enter, showing a crop’s recipients deliberately cut out of its yield.

The section asks a receiver to recognize the Rabb behind provision. After the garden is lost, the owners say “سبحان ربنا” and admit wrongdoing; their recognition makes explicit what the ingrate failed to acknowledge.
